blocks.text: Moving fluids have great importance. To find the behaviour of a fluid in motion we consider its flow through pipes. When a fluid is in motion its flow can take place in two ways, either streamline or turbulent.

blocks.title: Streamline flow
blocks.text: The flow is said to be streamline or laminar if every particle that passes a particular point moves along exactly the same path as the particles which passed that point earlier. In steady flow the motion of the particles is smooth and regular (Fig. 5.11); the smooth path followed by fluid particles in laminar flow is a streamline. A streamline may be straight or curved, and its tangent at any point gives the direction of flow of the fluid; different streamlines cannot cross each other.

blocks.alt: A pipe that is wide on the left and narrows smoothly to a narrow part on the right. Smooth streamlines run along it without crossing and come closer together in the narrow part. An arrow above shows the flow from left to right.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.11: Streamlines (laminar flow) (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.11).

blocks.text: A fluid flowing in a pipe (Fig. 5.12) has a certain velocity v1 at P, a velocity v2 at Q, and so on. If the velocity of a particle at P, Q and R does not change with the passage of time, the flow is steady flow or streamline flow. The line PQR representing the path followed by the particle is a streamline: the fixed path followed by orderly processing particles. In streamline flow all the particles passing through P also pass through Q and R, which means that two streamlines cannot cross each other.

blocks.alt: A gently curved pipe with one streamline drawn along it. At the points P, Q and R on the streamline, arrows v1, v2 and v3 show the velocities of the particles, each along the tangent to the streamline.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.12: The velocities of the particles at different points on streamline (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.12).

blocks.title: Turbulent flow
blocks.text: The irregular or unsteady flow of a fluid is called turbulent flow. Above a certain velocity the motion becomes unsteady and irregular and the velocity of the fluid changes abruptly (Fig. 5.13); the exact path of the particles cannot be considered. If two streamlines cross each other the particles go in one or the other direction and the flow is not steady: it is turbulent, with eddies and whirlpools in the motion and continuously changing paths.

blocks.alt: A flat black plate stands across a flow coming from the left. The middle flow line meets the plate; the lines above and below bend round its edges and then curl back towards the space behind the plate, forming eddies.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.13: Turbulent flow (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.13).

blocks.text: Formula One racing cars have a streamlined design, and dolphins have streamlined bodies to assist their movement in water (For Your Information).

items: The fluid is non-viscous: there is no frictional force between adjacent layers of the fluid.
The fluid is incompressible: its density is constant.

blocks.title: Rate of flow
blocks.text: The rate of flow of a fluid through a pipe is the volume of the fluid passing through any section of the pipe per unit time.

Consider a fluid flowing through a pipe of cross-sectional area A (Fig. 5.14) with velocity v for time t; the distance covered by the fluid in time t is l = v t, where l is the length of pipe the fluid passes through in time t. The volume passing through the pipe in time t is A x l = A v t, so the rate of flow of the liquid = volume / time = A v t / t = A v: rate of flow = A v ... (5.14). In SI units it is measured in cubic metres per second (m^3 s^-1), sometimes in litres per second (L s^-1).

blocks.alt: A pipe drawn as a long open cylinder of cross-sectional area A. Inside it a shaded column of fluid has length v x t, marked by a double arrow between two dashed lines below the pipe.
blocks.caption: Figure 5.14: Rate of flow of a liquid (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 5.14).

blocks.title: Steady flow
blocks.text: If the overall flow pattern does not change with time, the flow is called steady flow. In steady flow every particle of the fluid follows the same flow line as its previous particle.
